game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I think I got this for free some months ago and now got to play it. It ran rather fine on an Ubuntu 18.04 lapttop with Nouveau drivers, game has native Linux support. 
You play as a worker for a surveillance program, sorting through the web and accessing peoples devices, looking for clues about terrorists. I cant really compare the game to anything, maybe it is similar to a graphical novel to some extent, as you have limited choices, but you do have to use your head, even if the game pretty much always at least tells you where to look for clues.  
It was almost an initimate experience to look into the character life, their private chats and calls. I feel like they could have added a bit more "useless" webpages, to make the game more authentic, but it is obvious that they tried  to give their characters depth, which is where the game shines. 
As the name of the game tells us, to some extent it is obviously a political/ethical game, even if done rather abstract (you work for "the nation", and pretty much everyone you investigate did something wrong). 
One thing I really appreciated, was that they show what can happen if systems like this make mistakes, which is something I feel like is not discussed enough as a counterargument to surveillance, besides the obvious ethical ones.  Overall the the game is an interesting experience, but not comparable to games like "Spec Ops -  The Line", where you really have to get your hands dirty, which lessens the impression of consequences of the players actions in my opinion.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
When Orwell came out I was very intrigued by it, but from the screenshots, I wasn’t sure how it would be a game, recently my brother had recommended it to me as he knows my love for in depth and hard hitting story games. And I was not disappointed with this, it was in depth and definitely hard hitting where it counted and the only aspect of the game that I knew about when going into it, was the collection of information on people.

First things first, and quite briefly because there isn’t much to say about the graphics of the game. It is based on a user interface that you interact with, whilst it does emulate the use of an actual browser and its contents, it is very clean and takes the realistic nature away from it with its low poly style photos. This was a nice feature as I could focus more on what the story was offering than what the characters looked like and if the modeling of said characters worked with the rest of the interface. The only time there was animation was in the first cut scene where you were introduced to the game, however, this could be either 2D or 3D with flat colours and a low poly style to keep in with the theme. The only thing I was somewhat disappointed with was the fact that there was very little camera work, the game revolves around being monitored everywhere and it is constantly referenced to that cameras are a big thing, yet we do not experience this even though it was shown that they were capable of doing this. It did not, however, subtract from the story that there weren’t any cameras, it just would have been a pretty cool feature.

The graphics made it easy to navigate around the game, making the mechanics for the game very simple as you just had to click and drag certain pieces of information into a data bank, it was simple and easy to get to grips with, it just meant reading and doing a lot of problem solving. That, however, was the allure of the game, filling in the pieces and finding out just what was going on. Due to the dragging of information, you could affect the outcome of the game depending on what pieces of information you decided to let through, this was the coolest feature, I love multiple endings.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[i]Orwell[/i] is an episodic thriller involving the vulnerabilities of social media and easy access to critical digital information. You play as an employee of an NSA-like private government cyber-security agency called "Orwell", of course, named after George Orwell, and peep into your suspects' lives as you dig around for information that could tell if they are involved in anything that could put the lives of innocents in peril. The game is completely story-oriented, and at times, even choice-driven. 

[h1]Story:[/h1]

It's a thriller that follows the episode template like the [i]Telltale Games[/i], played as if you're a guy who's logged into his computer. Everything you do, see, or read is like as if you're logged into a computer. The story has a few interesting characters to read about, to peep into their lives and see just how much information you can dig up on them, and see how connected they are altogether. At times, you'll come across plot twists, and other kinds of ways the story could put you off with how you applied your actions by considering what you just saw right then first-hand, i.e., there may be more than meets the eye here. As the story progresses, the story gets deeper and darker, and your decisions will have to be considered more carefully. Sometimes, even the terms or choices given to you are there just to put you off. 

To me, I felt it drained down a bit when the whole plot unfolded, but it was pretty good overall. I haven't played the game extensively yet to see how many endings I could get, but there are indeed multiple endings. I don't dislike the endings that happen to you based on your choices. But the part of the story that you cannot change - the [b]huge[/b] plot twist - well, I didn't like it much. 

But more importantly, this game shows us just how exposed we are to everyone, and just how oblivious people are these days about this fact. It's pretty sci-fi, but who's to know that this could be our reality in a few years, give or take? We're slowly stumbling our way to a more surveilled future in which, you could say, we are going to live in an almost-communist digital world, where every singly word we type in the webs is taken for granted, and smeared on us as if we have anything troublesome to show for it. Hell, we go "Sorry, NSA" at times. So, in a way, we're just enjoying a false form of freedom. I could go into detail with how this is both good and bad, but this is only a game review, so... moving on. 

[h1]Visuals:[/h1]

The game looks like the people in it gave their own photos, and then they just used a heavily modified version of that Prisma app to convert it all to make it look like as it is. It's not bad. But, it kinda takes away the realism of it. I dunno if I could say it sits well with the tone of the game. I don't think it does. But, it's visually appealing. 

[h1]Mechanics & Gameplay:[/h1]

There's very little to no mechanics. Having the whole investigative thing in the game, it surely  calls for implementing the use of the keyboard. The devs could've considered adding search terms and stuff, but sadly, this mechanic wasn't added to the game, and that, too, takes away the realism from the game. Something like, if you can't find something in the game that you're looking for, that's related to a certain character, search the appropriate term up, and find it (like [i]Her Story[/i]). That's what would make it more engaging, because there's no knowing what you could possibly find. Clicking and dragging can get stale. Hopefully, if they make a follow-up to [i]Orwell[/i], they could implement this.

In the sense of gameplay, it's pretty interesting. As you play, you come across multiple choices to make. You're basically making choices constantly. When you have an info that you have the choice of either using it or not, you will probably think of the following:

"Do I drag this information to the profile?"
"[i]Should[/i] I drag this information to the profile?"
"How does this information have an effect?"
"Is this info even worth putting into the files?"

A simple statement that has to do something with the character - you will think it about in a much deeper manner. Because when you do enter something, it gets reflected on the reports, and that could have a cause-and-effect thing going on. The "choices matter" tag on this game is appropriate. And that's the whole point of the game. You, as an investigator, must see to it that everything you do in this works out perfectly in the end, for the people in Orwell, as well as the public.

[h1]Music:[/h1]

The music fits well with the theme of the game, it's sci-fi-y, it gives off the mysterious vibe, and if you see a plot twist, the music suddenly changes to a very tense, "oh damn" type of tone. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

If all you do in a game is walk, then you call it a "walking simulator". This game is that. All you mostly do is click and drag stuff. Which makes it a "clicking simulator". But, it's appropriate, because you can't really do much with a computer other than click and drag and type, can you? 

Funny (lol, not) jokes aside, the premise of the game is solid, and how they elaborate on it, with you as the very thing that gets to use what's given to you against those [b]like[/b] us. Just imagine if this happened ([b][i]*cough*ishappening*cough*[/i][/b]) in real life. The primary focus of the game was definitely the story, and the story only. The replayability of the game relies on the achievements, and the multiple endings present in the game (for most, even trading cards).

I recommend this game to story lovers, I don't recommend this game to those who get bored of simple mechanics, and I recommend you get this game during the sales. I enjoyed the story a lot, but, I wanted more to do than just clicking and dragging. There's a [i]f-i-i-i-ne[/i] grey area between those two, and I'm right smack in the middle of it. But, being a game that focuses entirely on the story, and the kind of message it's trying to interpret to us, I give it a thumbs up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A poignant game on the times we live in. I'm a humongous fan of the "Walking Simulator" genre and I stumbled upon this game during the Steam Winter Sale (3 days ago). Orwell has a captivating storyline that takes the "first person" experience quite literally. Without spoiling the game, the story focuses on a user operated software called Orwell, where the player assumes the role as a operator outside the fictatious "Nation", spying on activists that are tagged as potentially violent. 

The user interface is streamlined, dare I say "user-friendly". The fictional profiles depicted in the video game are unnervingly real, pulling me into the experience, as though as I really am spying on others. The characters are well scripted, albeit being scripts of text. The characters are caricatures of stereotypical activists, with complex backgrounds and hidden agendas. 

The "orwellian" connotations that are hinted at in the game are subtle, nuanced without being too overbearing or obvious. As you progressively submit information on labelled targets, you start to feel a heavy burden of responsibility on your shoulders. The multiple options and consequences from submitting false information add more weight to the situation. The activities or rituals performed by the main character are a frighteningly realistic, depecting the state of the world we live in. 

My only complaints include the duration of the game: it is rather short in length, more like a concept game showcasing some of the developer's strengths. The waiting times between each mission is abysmal, sometimes resulting in multiple crashes. 

All in all, this is an underrated gem in the walking simulator category, standing tall with the likes of Gone Home and Soma.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's okay. I'm really torn on this one. There are aspects that are cool. It does make you feel like you are really part of an all-powerful government spying agency, and it did make me feel guilty for what I did at times, which is kinda the point. So in that regard I think the game achieved what it set out to. 

However, the gameplay wasn't that fun to me. The choices that you are given are pretty mundane, and some of them don't even make sense. I played it while drunk once, and I sat there for like 20 minutes trying to decide between two options, analyzing the semantics, because both were technically false depending on how you look at it. Eventually I just stopped caring and chose whatever struck me at the moment because sometimes there is no logical answer that takes all the facts into account. Your choices do have an impact for sure, but because of the wording of some of the options, it isn't really clear what you are choosing. Given that it is basically a visual novel, I wouldn't expect the gameplay to be amazing. But I would at least hope for some robust choices, and a riveting storyline. Well, while the premise is interesting, the actual storyline involves mostly frivolous details about the characters and their lives without really making me bond enough with any of them to actually care all that much, so it ended up being kinda boring after the novelty wore off, honestly.

Also, I have to say I didn't really find the world they built very believable. They basically portrayed a totalitarian police state world within the framework of our existing politics to some degree, and it doesn't really make sense. For example, the terrorists all seem to be left wing communist types. Fair enough. But they are kinda portrayed in a positive light, like they are fighting for freedom. But really, they don't want freedom, it seems they idolize communist dictators, so they just want THEIR side to be the totalitarian state. Which makes sense in a way, but then why all the rhetoric about freedom? If you want communism, you really don't care about freedom. And they portray the totalitarian government as conservative. Interesting choice, given that modern conservatives are the ones speaking up for free speech and lower taxes and stuff. Oh yeah, and the totalitarian government wants to lower taxes. Umm, okay? If you have a totalitarian government that can rule with an iron fist, why bother lowering taxes? Don't you need lots of money so you can have all these government programs to run people's lives? As a bit of a politics junkie, the way they built the political landscape has a lot of ideological inconsistencies, is basically what I am saying. I'm not saying it's impossible that there would be a conservative totalitarian regime. But that would come with a specific set of beliefs. They wouldn't be pushing for family values for example. Ever read "Brave New World"? Defeating the family and community structures is key to politically subjugating the population. I could go on, but basically, because of the inconsistencies, I found myself being pulled out of the experience.

Also, there is some weird plot point that tries to tie in this semi-fictional, semi-real world into the actual real world? That part is pretty confusing and I think they could have left it out because it doesn't add anything IMO and it just makes less sense the more you think about it. I think they should have gone all in on a completely fictional world, with a completely different society instead of trying to tie it in in weird ways like making the terrorists left wing punk rock vegan types, and the totalitarian government conservative family types, with all the baggage that comes along with those stereotypes. Think about 1984 and Brave New World. I'm pretty sure that the authors went out of their ways to make sure that no political archetypes were projected onto the characters because that would take people out of the story and into debates about modern-day politics. They would have done well to do the same here. Just make a broader point without muddying the waters with tribalism.

Honestly, I would probably give it a 5.5/10. It's interesting for a little while, so I guess it's good that it's not very long. I had no desire to play it over and see different endings, frankly I was a bit relieved when it was over. So, maybe I should be giving it a hesitant thumbs up... But because I'm so torn on it, and the other reviews are so positive, I'm gonna have to give it a thumbs down to get it closer to where I think it should be.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is so-so; I want to recommend something *like* Orwell, but I'm on the fence about recommending Orwell itself. The game raises interesting issues, and the world would indeed be better off if everyone had at least the simulated experience of working with a large-scale surveillance system. I even usually found the story compelling, and I finished the game. However, the execution also felt a little disappointing.

The main gameplay problem, in my experience, was that sometimes I felt forced to take random or stupid-seeming actions just to see what it was that would finally advance the plot. This was in spite of the "handholding" cues the game uses to help you along.

Another thing that bothered me was a set of accuracy/realism concerns, which I will go on about below.

*************************************************

(Optional section about accuracy)

My main objection is that the game gives a poor sense of what doing an investigation with help of an Orwell-like system would actually be like in real life. In real life, either A) the computer would be a very powerful autonomous system and would make conclusions without human or involvement; or B) the human researcher would have sensible basic capabilities such as updating information, correcting machine-extracted snippets, and supplementing files with written analysis. The game tries to be somewhere in between, and in the process makes something that's unrealistic and sometimes annoying.  Also, there were also moments of "what the heck does the game want from me now", when I would add pointless or even incorrect information to the Orwell database solely to see if it would finally be the thing to move the plot forward.

The fact that you can't modify information in the Orwell crime database is pretty stupid on the face of things. To be fair, though, maybe it stands metaphorically for problems that could actually arise. For example, if two government agencies had a file on you, but the two were not in sync, the fact that you're not actually a criminal could be updated in one department's file without the second department learning about this, and perhaps the second database could lead to your extrajudicial killing.

The contextless, overaly literal way that information is passed from investigator to police is completely absurd. Perhaps this is a useful reflection of one possible way that an agency using an Orwell-type system could be dysfunctionally structured, though you'd hope that a bureaucracy wouldn't be quite that stupid. Or perhaps this limited information passing is symbolic of a potentially problem where two crime databases were linked, but could only communicate back and forth using a limited, contextless technical vocabulary, which would perpetuate misunderstanding. 

Perhaps the point of the game, though, is not to be right about the *particulars* of what could go wrong in a mass surveillance system, but more to give people an accessible experience that gives a general sense of creepiness.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Product received for free on Humble Bundle GIveaway[/h1]

So I got this game for free on HB, and was eager to try it out. As I am a fan of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopia]dystopian[/url] novels and games. Fictions like [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four]1984[/url] or [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brave_New_World]Brave New World[/url] are what I'd love to read.

This game is based off George Orwell's 1984(hence the game's name [i]Orwell[/i]). A government launching a surveillance system in a bid to stop "terrorists" and their "attacks". You are one of the agents that helps submitting [i]correct[/i] information to government intel. Suspects will be arrested or able to escape from arrestments based on what information you provided. Much like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/agecheck/app/475550/]Beholder[/url], you can save innocents or those you want to help by not submitting certain data to the Orwell system.

After a few minutes into the game, I decide that this game is quite worth the pennies. It allows you to experience being a "Big Brother" - watching citizens behind, logging every moves they make, and determining their ultimate fate. Although the Big Brother perspective is already popular among dystopian games. I find this one quite interesting. Unlike beholder, you don't need to go around maintaining good terms with residents. Instead you sit right in front of a surveillance system, pretty much like the real world NSA agents would do in their everyday work.

To sum up, I would recommend this game to everyone. Still thinking your privacy is REALLY SAFE online? On the fence of thinking about being spyed on? Play this game.

review_text_raw:
[i] *very, very minor spoilers are hidden* [/i]

[h1] TL;DR "The Last Enemy" without Cucumberpatch [/h1]

Admittedly, the above reference might skate over a few people's heads, but the core themes are the same. Based loosely around the old US Total Information Awareness system, the game explores the issues around predictive profiling and human bias.

The details are what makes this game shine: The irrelevant online junk, the typos and slang, the shoddy dating websites, even the pages load like a real browser. The user interface is slick and easy to use. For that extra immersion, I really recommend taking your time to read as much as you can. It's not as quirky as DX:HR, but it's close.

The characters are wonderfully complex, if occasionally stereotypical. I love the "show, don't tell" approach of implying their personalities through online interactions, and the format of the game is really unique -- I've never played a game quite like this before.

My biggest gripe is gameplay. There is none. Everything is highlighted and every conflict displayed, which underwhelms the idea that [spoiler] your bias invalidates Orwell [/spoiler], and eventually turns the game into a mindless point-and-click. There are no difficult puzzles or decisions beyond moral ones, and even those seem to have little bearing on the outcome. The ending certainly felt a little shoehorned, and the [spoiler] twist a little out of character [/spoiler]. It's best to view this game as an interactive story rather than a game. I'd have also liked the ability to replay individual episodes - restarting the game just to change a single decision in ep. 5 is a little inconvenient.

As a very fast reader, the entire game took 3-4 hours to complete, bearing in mind I read absolutely everything. Half the time seems to be spent on watching conversations scroll in real time, which is realistic, but not for the impatient. If you don't like reading or text-based games, don't bother.

I really do recommend this game. The tense, compelling plot had me eagerly waiting for the next episode. You do become emotionally involved with the characters, even with a week between episodes. A little shallow at times, but enjoyable nonetheless.

11/10 would hack the local fishing society again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation. ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.” Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of. Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600 and out of the many games I have played only 5  have inspired me to award them my own personal score of 10. Orwell has joined this very exclusive list for me. The game is a masterclass of using the medium of video games to make poignant social commentary that feels gripping and authentic. 

Daniel Marx (Game Designer) is a fantastic writer who gives each one of his characters a very distinct voice using colloquial dialogue and expressions that stay consistent for each character throughout the course of the 5 chapters of the story. His ability to create believable characters with personalities and motivations that feel real is the key to making the message of the game resonate. This isn't a simple story of noble heroes and evil villains, this is an examination of complex people and their struggles to reconcile their beliefs and their feelings, their fears and their ability to summon up the courage to do what they feel is right. 

The Gameplay is simple to understand, but choices made by the player do have branching consequences. Reminiscent of Telltale games and other members of the narrrative genre with a choice driven structure. The game manages to give the player a sense of real agency in the outcomes of the story, and have genuinley significant differences at several key moments. My mind spins at the challenge of writing a story that is able to stay consistent throughout its length, and yet offer a significant number of alternatives that need to be followed to their logical conclusion. Again, my compliments to Daniel Marx on his writing skills and game design. Impressive. Very impressive. 

The art style reminded me of the polygonal look of games like Out of This World and Flashback from the early and mid 90's with improved technology that looks good and yet remains accessible to all players even ones with 8 year old laptops (such as myself). Compliments to Melanie Taylor for an aesthetic that is easy on the eye and hardware. 

In the end, the writing, gameplay and art all serve to execute on making a statement about the ever increasing surveillance that is taking place in our own world and it is no suprise that the invasion of privacy that is possible at this very moment is something that can chill to the bone. We are at a crossroads in the story of humanity, whether the next chapters are dominated by the decision to sacrifice freedom for security or the acceptance that freedom carries risks, but is far better than a world where everyone is always suspect of being an enemy of the state and a target for elimination. 

Provided you do not object to reading a great deal (as there is no voice acting), this game will provide you with 10 hours of riveting narrative that will undoubtedly leave you questioning how much autonomy we are willing to surrender for the illusion of safety that a large surveillance state seemingly affords. 

I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

P.S. Additionally many thanks to Michael Kluge (Programming) for his coding work. The game runs very well. Amazing that this trio of developers crafted such a landmark title. I bow to your triumvirate of talent. 

P.P.S : Incidentally, in case anyone is interested, my other Perfect 10 games are :

- Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time
- Resident Evil 4
- Batman : Arkham City
- Last of Us
- Telltale's The Walking Dead : Season 1

Very different from Orwell, but masterpieces for me in the revolution in video game design they brought to different elements of the industry.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I own 457 games.

None have been as engrossing or as thought provoking as Orwell was. Evocative, powerful and moving and an accurate commentary considering the gradual erosion of digital privacy rights in the modern world.

Not so much a game, as a bold political statement that allows the 'player' to draw their own conclusions on whether security is worth privacy and whether peace should come at the price of freedom.

It certainly lives up to it's name.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible


Cons:
- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.
- Game lasts no more than 8 hours.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: great game buggered by stupid save system. 

Orwell is a great game, no two ways about it. Easy to get into, nice story and so forth. I didn't have a problem with any of those things, however why have I then thumbed it down? 

Simple, this game, like so many others nowadays, have decided that the only save function this game needs is an autosave, meaning there is no way of backtracking, no way of re-doing things. One slip up and the game will laugh in your face and call you a tosser for the rest of the game, because that slip-up meant you didn't achieve what you wanted to do. I know some people are okay with that, they feel it's more immersive or whatever, but for me it is just a huge annoyance. "Realism" is all well and good, but they don't make the chat convos ingame take 5 minutes per post because while that'd be realistic, it's be annoying. For me it is the same thing here and it leaves me unable to really enjoy the game because it screws me over when I can't decide which of the two vague clues are the correct one. 

It is a crying shame, it's a great game but the save system isn't fun for me at all.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

In the final act, you see written in what characters have said choices for an outcome. However, it is not clear how you are supposed to enact what I imagine for most players would be the desired outcome, nor does the character's explanation of how that outcome shall come about make sense.

Despite all of the references to Orwell's 1984, the comparison between The Nation and Oceania would be a lazy one. This is a game to suit someone who has only heard of 1984, and not actually read it. Where the extent of their understanding of the work is that that Big Brother fellow liked his surveillance. 

In the game, The Nation is authoritarian, but non-ideological. There is something about it being pro-interventionist and anti-immigration, but this does not serve as an effective allegory about real-world politics. Although the beastly Orwell programme reaches far into people's private lives, its administrators are awfully concerned with ethics and the rule of law. They have to gain legal warrants to bring someone under the scrutiny of the system, and are annoyed by your giving them extraneous personal detail. 

Although some important legal protections for the accused are absent, accused people are apparently entitled to legal representation. There is no indication that the state much cares about what people think, or that it coerces them into changing. That is, there are no thought crimes in The Nation, and state power is not arbitrary or lawless. Rather, its inhabitants appear to have have freedom of speech, thought and assembly (and, it seems from one plot point, the right to bear arms).

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I am really conflicted on this game.
On one hand, it looks and sounds excellent, being extremely stylish and immersing the player into a dystopian world of total surveillence, the characters being (mostly) well-written and felt alive. All the websites, social networks, advertisement banners and the online banter is very realistic, they even included some made-up memes for their made-up world that looked like something that could actually exist in ours. Also, had a high-quality localisation to my native language (Russian) and i didn't really feel like i was missing anything out by not playing it in its original language.

Now, on the other hand. This game mostly play out like a visual novel, where you make your choices in whether or not to upload a certain bit of marked information into the system. There are also bits with "conflicting facts" in which you also can make a choice that can affect how will the story develop. And, for the most of the game, yor choices do matter: will a certain character go to jail or manage to escape the police? Will you frame someone who made a minor break of the law into something more incriminating, so he will actually get arrested? It is incredubly nice: as a player, you feel the real power of someone with the tools for total surveillence, with only your own morals that might prevent you from abusing that power. 
The story itself plays out nicely, keeping the player in suspence, with enough of "Oh god" moments to keep you invested... right until its final part. For me, it really felt like the game did a U-turn and started pushing its morals on me, instead of letting me, as a player, to make the final choice. Sure, there are multiple endings, but all of them mostly convey the same idea (no spoilers), which, i felt, was insulting to all the choices i made before it. I expected it to be more "morally-grey", especially considering how well it started, but in the end it tried to be a lesson in how you should think. And those very same people tell us about thought crimes? Ironic.

Not recommended, unless you are fine with the game's morale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Remember Spycraft: The Great Game? It was this weird mostly live-action-video adventure game that came on 4 cds back in the 90s, and tasked you to roll up an international conspiracy using your wits and a bunch of cool digital tools.

It played off "real" intelligence work, sifting through documents, collecting tidbits of data.

Orwell is a lot like that, but with just the digital shenanigans, played out in an age when the NSA sees you naked and knows who you're gossipping about.

I like it a lot, although it also kinda makes me miss the bits of Spycraft that felt realistic. Like sifting through a document in search of a password or a connection, having to really notice and remember details, and then piecing it all together yourself. 

It worked your brain and engaged you in a way that Orwell doesn't, but Orwell is so well put together that it makes up the difference. It keeps you hooked on the story and the taboo of looking through these peoples lives, sort of tapping into the "Facebook stalker" experience, thinking "God, what a loser" while you're tracing some two-bit musicians path into terrorism.

There are a couple of minor shortcomings though. There's no voice acting on phonecalls, sometimes you find relevant datapoints and you can't use them simply because they don't have "The Outline", and the conflict system can be a bit obtuse, not unlike the Lie/Doubt thing in LA Noire, which is frustrating, but never enough to bring the game down.

So if you want that experience of losing your soul in the service of a faceless controller-state that gives absolutely no fucks about you, then Orwell is about as good as it gets. Happy hunting, you mindless serfs!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Examples of games with a good save system for this style of gameplay include [i]A Wolf Among Us[/i] and [i]Papers, Please.[/i][/strike]

[b]A bit linear, limited.[/b] There were some moments I wish some bit of text was highlighted (you may only drag and upload highlighted data chunks) since I wanted to explore that avenue of inquiry, but [i]Orwell[/i] had other plans. This gave the game a restricted feeling. It does not leave the game open to a world of naturally-occurring red herrings (only game-constructed ones, not user constructed), which I think would have added much more depth to the game. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A fun little document reading simulator.

Seriously, that is the gameplay. It's like a season of 24, where you have to find out where the bomb is going to go off, and it's all up to you, but instead of an elite anti-terrorist agent, you're some rando sitting in front of a PC, hired to sift through documents. That is literally who you are, in the universe of the game. You submit portions of documents to the system, and this unlocks more documents. That may sound a little silly, but the game explains itself pretty well.

No need to worry about 'pixel hunting' or broken logic - all problems are solved and the plot is progressed in all cases by finding the right entry in the right document. If anything, the game holds your hand. 

You can only submit portions of any document that the system deems potentially relevant. You cannot get a game over - you could play this game through by blindly submitting every bit of highlighted text you found, without paying attention to the plot.

But the plot itself is worth paying attention to - a slow-burn story of a parallel world with technology from five minutes into the future. That lawyer guy on youtube who rates the legal accuracy of various pieces of pop culture would probably not rate this thing too highly. But it is fun, and the rationale for everything that happens is internally consistent.

There are branching paths and different outcomes to minor plot points, as well as alternate endings, depending on how you play  - which boils down to which pieces of information you choose to submit or not submit. It is worth the second and even third play-throughs needed to explore every possible outcome.

Which brings me to my two main complaints:

- There is a checkpoint system, limited to the five main chapters/days of the campaign. You can replay a previous day/chapter, but as soon as you start say, chapter two, your progress in the remaining 3 chapters is lost.

- There is no fast-track buttons for voice or text conversations - they play out in real time, complete with 'realistic' pauses, whether you like it or not.

Neither of these are game-breaking, and are more just quality of life features that I found to be conspicuously absent. Their absence mean that secondary playthroughs for achievements/branch discovery take a little longer than they otherwise would.

I bought Orwell on sale, and went in to it without doing much homework, but I got the impression that this would be several distinct yet related cases. It's more like one big ongoing case. Also in contrast to the Ace Attorney games, which Orwell reminds me of just a little, the plot is a little more serious, and the characters a little less colorful. But if you like that series, or sifting through documents to find a terrorist in a dystopian alternate world sounds like fun to you, and if none of what I have written sounds like a deal-breaker, and you find this game at a price that you think is worth ten or so hours of gameplay, go for it.

One final thought - this game is about a surveillance state, but it doesn't take the easy way out. It poses the dilemma of government overreach/corruption for 'safety' vs. privacy/freedom concerns in an interesting way. I would not say that Orwell is quite as brilliant or profound as some of the glowing reviews suggest, but I do like the way that the plot, the gameplay, and the endings you are able to choose all come together to get you thinking about this issue, even if just a little.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Ultimately, my review comes down to one question:  "Would I pay for this?"  The answer is, no I don't think I would.  I can certainly see where this game would appeal to some, but it doesn't to me.  Hence, the negative score.  I don't regret playing it for free, but I don't think I would have been missing out had I not played it.

Orwell is a story game, first and foremost.  It has somewhat non-linear story to tell, where your actions will affect the details of the plot, but it'll otherwise run more or less the same, and you'll have a choice of three or four endings depending on how you do the finale.  The game tries to cover the problem of survellience but... IMO, it misses the mark completely when the tools used to spy are... indept.  More on that later.

The game boils down to reading fictional internet pages, spying on emails, calls, and texts, and snooping on people's computers.  Your goal is to find "important" information, that is pre-highlighted for you, and drag and drop what you feel is important.  The game stresses that you try to pick correct and relevant information but, ultimately, there's no failure state.  Being accurate or inaccurate only affects the plot details, nothing else, and kinda underminds the engagement of what little gameplay there is.

There's major problems with this though.  You're an investigator on a case, but your partner and the tools you're using are inept.  You can supply information, but you're often not allowed to include the context too.  Context is stupid important in real investigations, so it really undermines, well, the whole system.  You'll also come across "conflicting data", sometimes before you've even found the info it conflicts with.  A good investigator would record it all and then review it later and dismiss what's incorrect.  In Orwell?  You have to pick one.  And sometimes you have to pick blindly.  Just... why?  You also cannot collect information on individuals related to the main suspects, something I figure would be rather important.

It'll also leave you wondering one major question:  what sort of security and surveillance dystopia doesn't even have basic information, such as dates of birth and known addresses, already on file?  For a government trying to imitate 1984's Big Brother, they're failing hard at it.  Especially when around 75% of the information you're gathering is from public sources...

This here's the whole problem:  the game tries to make you question whether government observation is good or bad and whether things should be more private.  But then it puts you in the role of a guy who spends a lot of the time collecting publicly posted information and digging up stuff slower than a Google search.  Snooping into calls, computers, and bank accounts is certainly fishy, yeah, but nothing that would be legally off-limits to a police officer with a warrant in Real Life™.  And considering the plot... warrants are totally justified for everyone involved.

Orwell tries, and the story is just interesting enough for a 3-4 hour playthrough.  But... the political discussion just falls flat due to its own gameplay.  And there's games that are much better at hunting down and acquiring your information without highlighting it for you, like the parts of Hacknet focused on snooping.  

IMO:  not really worth the buy.  If you're really curious, try the demo and if you still want it, wait for a sale.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

Overall, "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" is a masterpiece that not only entertains but also makes you think. It is a game that stays with you long after you have finished playing. I highly recommend it to anyone looking for an intelligent and captivating game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Guys!  Perhaps this may come as a shock to some of you but, in case you didn’t know, this game has a bit of an agenda….[/b] 
Ok ok, joking aside I bought Orwell a while back when it fell below my “if I buy this and don’t like it, I won’t feel any great loss” threshold.  It sat in my library untouched until a rainy day when I didn’t feel like getting into anything too involved.  I say this to admit that I went into this with pretty bland expectations.  

I generally view games like this the way I do a book from an unknown author, but that has a premise I like.  I knew going in that the game makers had a point to make and even though it was a point I generally agree with, I was a little wary.  [i]I don’t like being preached at, so I wasn’t sure if I was going to spend the entire game being beat over the head with the rhetoric bat whilst being presented with billboards saying in big bold letters “Hey look, the authors feel very strongly about this” at every turn or if the game would have any merit beyond the political statement.[/i]  [b]I’m very thankful to say that this game was far more than just a tray upon which to serve political and social commentary and it was even very clever in doing so.[/b]

So why did I start out with all that waffle about political commentary?  Because I want to set the tone for how I approached the game and the preconceptions I had going in.  I went into the experience thinking that I pretty much had them figured out and that I would easily be able to see through any “hard choices with lasting consequences” to what the authors were really trying to sell to the player.  And chapter 1 pretty much was just that.  I “knew” they were trying to get me to suspect a particular person and that they wanted me to assume the simple answer so they could jump out from behind the posterized, low-polygon trees and say “Ha!  See how even with all the information at your fingertips you jumped to the wrong conclusion.”  So naturally I did just the opposite.  Purposefully ignoring what I assumed were red-herrings and by the end of chapter 1, I’d almost lost interest figuring that I had it all figured out.  I was delighted, and a bit disappointed, that I was wrong.  

Starting chapter 2, I was actually engaged in the narrative and was now determined not to be caught off-guard again.  I still knew there was a point to it all, but I wasn’t as sure I knew what that point was.  By the end of the game, I knew what was going on, but because I’d fed information to orwell earlier on that seemed harmless at the time, I’d built a profile on some of the characters that was not incorrect but was misrepresentative.  This led to events playing out in a way that I didn’t want and with no way to go back and correct.  I felt duped, but in a good way.  The game had indeed gotten it’s point across, but in a very subtle and engaging way that left me still feeling that I enjoyed the experience.

So let’s sum this up, shall we? 
•	Orwell was well worth the money
•	Gameplay was not nearly as on-rails as I had expected
•	Story was actually very engaging and believable
•	Plot twists did not feel super-contrived simply to force the player to be wrong for the sake of proving a point.  All the plot twists could have been seen coming I think if the user had paid attention to the details and not just focused on what Orwell highlights.
•	The game actually made me think and didn’t preach it’s point smugly from contrived moral high-ground and I appreciated that.  

Here is where I would usually list a few things that could have been improved, but the game is pretty simple and the UI layout is simple and easy to use.  Some of the “websites” that you visit have clickable links that aren’t obvious… that was kind of annoying, but not too bad.  I’d like to say that I wish you could go back and edit information when you found out it was wrong, but I think it’s integral to the game the concept that YOU are the filter.  If it’s not relevant, accurate, or then you don’t upload it.  If I had one complaint it would be that I sometimes didn’t know what would “trigger” the next event and so sometimes I’d upload something I didn’t really want to just because I thought I had to in order to progress the game.   

All in all, the game took me about 6 hours to play through… you could go longer or shorter, but in the end, it’s not a great investment timewise…. In fact, it practically gives you a good stopping point between chapters.  I highly recommend the game.  It’s worth $7-10 for your time and as a good conversation starter.  Gift it to a friend so you can have a good conversation on the topic.  

Anyway, That’s my 2 cents worth.

-John
