game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] A very enjoyable game with hidden depth, despite the very simple game mechanics. [/h1]

You investigate persons of interest in a bombing (i.e read a whole bunch and invade peoples' privacy) through their online information and electronic devices via Orwell, The Nations new secret surveilence system. The people and ways you can investigate are not all immediately available, you unlock more options and imformation based on the data you upload and where you are in the story. The gameplay ultimately boils down to drag-and-droping the datachunks (that the game hightlights) that you think are relevent, into Orwell.

While on the surface the game may seem not very challenging or lacking in replayability as some claim, there are subtleties that make Orwell really great.

Such as the fact that you, as the investigator, are the only person who will see the [b] context [/b] of the data you're uploading. Mild episode 1 spoiler: [spoiler] See a woman joking with her boyfriend that she stole his credit card (which she uses to buy a bottle of wine), which he seems mildly annoyed by but seemingly fine with? Upload that into Orwell and all your superiors know is that she "stole a credit card". [/spoiler] Whether or not you think reporting that is morally right or not, it does have an effect on how things turn out for her.
There are several times such as this when the information you can upload is damning, incomplete or inaccurate simply because the datachunk lacks context. There are times when you can use this to your advantage, if say you want to frame someone winkwink.

There are also times where you will encounter "conflicting data chunks", where you have the choice of which one (sometimes if any) you wish to upload. These choices often lead to a person or circumstance being viewed in an entirely different manner. Sometimes it is the drastic difference between someone being seen as a terrorist or an innocent.
This is why it's very important to look very carefully at what a datachunk is really uploading to Orwell and remember you needn't and perhaps shouldn't upload everything.

Overall this game puts you into a position where you have to make a lot of moral decisions around privacy, relevancy, and generally be the judge of everyone you investigate. Your choices/ethics directly and indirectly influence the fate of all the characters you meet.

A brief note on replayability: I found there to be plenty of reasons to replay the game; be it for achievement hunting, because you messed up a lot the first time around (like me ^-^'), or just to see how everything pans out if you'd played differently. As of writing I have 11.3 hours on record and I still intend to play it further as I don't feel remotely done yet.
How much time you'll get out of it depends a lot on your playstyle and whether you're a completionist or someone who blitzes through games and doesn't bother with a replay.
The average time to finish your first run through seems to be around 4 or 5 hours for most people.

tldr: Tbh as long as you like detective and/or story-driven games, I whole-heartedly recommend Orwell. While I got it on sale, since playing I would totally pay full price.

P.S Try the demo because if you get to the end of it and feel the overwelming need to keep playing, you'll enjoy the full game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This is not a bad game, but I do think it's overrated. It falls short as a game and as a study of the surveillance state.

The gameplay mechanics are very simple -- you go to different links and and decide whether to upload them to Orwell or not. That's all there is to gameplay. Frustratingly, I ran into a few occasions where to advance the story I had to upload a link that was not obvious as to its value. Additionally, it's silly that you can't correct events later on, even before the information is acted upon -- if you send something over it's set in stone. And I'm not talking about the conflict choices -- those actually were good and created a good choice to have to make in deciding how the fate of certain people would go. 

Some of those negatives really betrayed the gamey-ness of the system. 

But worse was the whole conceit of the game really misses on being a meditation of surveillance gone awry. For one, the investigator is not a member of The Nation, which simply wouldn't happen in the real world, so it undercuts the influence of the government. The pressure that you as the investigator feels is thus negligble (unlike something like Papers, Please). The artificiality of the Orwell setup avoids the influence of government on media or bias of investigators that is very much an issue in the real world. 

Additionally, the game seems to suggest that the mere possibility of some people being investigated without having done wrong is evil. Except, that is how criminal investigations have gone since time immemorial. You start with some clues and investigate from there which will inevitably lead to some innocent people being scrutinized (even sometimes convicted). But that is the outcome of such a human operation and is not really a result of the surveillance state. And remember, we're investigating actual crimes where innocent people died. 

The game would have been much stronger if it showed intentional abuse by the system operators, influence by the government, or the ability to enact control of a population by knowing the way they think and act (think machine learning and how well it can predict certain behaviors/beliefs in people now). Or if the act in question was more dubious in nature, was maybe a false flag, or at least had some element of a frame up instead of an actual terrorist act committed by a true believer.

Another minor gripe is that you can't skip ahead on any chat or phone calls, which are interminably slow. While that might be realistic, it's also a bit boring.

The story also provides choices and branches in the same manner as a Telltale game, so if you like that facade you won't be bothered here. However, I did find it a bit unsatisfying that no matter the choices you made, the next episode would essentialy go the same way. And since everything is told in documents, calls, and chats, it's really lacking the dramatic power that a good Telltale game can have.

It wasn't a bad time but I definitely felt underwhelmed.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It’s timely that Orwell, the first game from Australian start-up Osmotic Studios delves into the muddy waters of government surveillance of its citizens, with the increasing nature of real world democracies doing the very same as they grapple with a world that is always connected and communicating.

Orwell opens with a deadly bombing in a public square that the player is tasked to investigate. This is achieved via a secret program codenamed Orwell, which allows an anonymous user, with the oversight of a supervisor, to snoop through social media posts, personal computers, bank statements and private correspondence of the suspects and associates.

My initial surveillance began with a singular suspect who had been caught by CCTV in the surrounding area and who had previously been arrested for attacking a police officer. My supervisor seemed to believe in this system, that malice lurked in unseen corners and that everyone was a potential threat.

From this one suspect a deeper conspiracy of activists emerged, and concerns of the erosion of liberties that were taken for granted by the citizens both fortified and weakened the idea of Orwell.

Continuing to spy on the fellow member’s activist group Thought reveals snippets of conversation that follow a story of mistrust of government and the over-reach of surveillance. Your actions, and inaction can and do have major consequences for those that you survey – and decisions on what you choose to upload to Orwell through a simple drag and drop interface can have fatal consequences and lock you to certain storylines.

Sifting through the large amount of data that the unknowing citizens freely make available reveals a story of love, betrayal, anger and sacrifice. I could have skipped this text – foregone most of the pertinent information. Highlighted text makes it easy to ascertain what is applicable to your current investigations. But this is to the game’s detriment – and the story woven is well worth your time.

Orwell paints a plausible microcosm of our online habits, with mirrors of Facebook, Twitter and chat logs providing a certain narcissistic perspective of how we perceive the world. These characters are fleshed out people, and the media puppet is scathingly presented as acting only in its self-interest. This is hilariously presented at moments, such as when it gives nothing by positive press to a major advertiser, even when your own investigations show there is moral outrage at their actions.

The highlighted information well can occasionally dry up, and you might have to recheck what you missed, but the six hour journey is worth the effort. Minor shortcomings in its design aside, Orwell provides a relatively gripping story of interactive fiction where whatever you upload, even the most trivial, can change the course of the story and of your understanding of it.

Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. 

The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time.

8.2/10.

I could have skipped this text – foregone most of the pertinent information. Highlighted text makes it easy to ascertain what is applicable to your current investigations. But this is to the game’s detriment – and the story woven is well worth your time. Orwell paints a plausible microcosm of our online habits, with mirrors of Facebook, Twitter and chat logs providing a certain narcissistic perspective of how we perceive the world. These characters are fleshed out people, and the media puppet is scathingly presented as acting only in its self-interest. This is hilariously presented at moments, such as when it gives nothing by positive press to a major advertiser, even when your own investigations show there is moral outrage at their actions. The highlighted information well can occasionally dry up, and you might have to recheck what you missed, but the six hour journey is worth the effort. Minor shortcomings in its design aside, Orwell provides a relatively gripping story of interactive fiction where whatever you upload, even the most trivial, can change the course of the story and of your understanding of it. Orwell highlights the overarching issue of the choice between liberty and intrusion and how that plays out can weigh heavily on the decisions you make throughout the game. Something as minor as anxiety medication that is snooped from a suspect’s medical files leads the suspect to be targeted as unstable. It’s only a small leap from there to classify them as dangerous. We have nothing to fear if we have nothing to hide – and the ability to be able to follow these disparate people, through their online social interactions is a fascinating journey that I am really glad I took. The dilemma of authority versus autonomy shifts rapidly in a world that is under threat - and a game like Orwell, an interactive fiction no less, shows there is a lot more about us online than we may realise or care to know. Indeed, by the game’s end I was questioning what I knew about what information I had freely shared. That Orwell can have you re-examine your life is a testament to the present reality. It’s a great game, and well worth your time. 8.2/10.

review_text_raw:
[h1] "For The Nation, for the security of the citizens, for their safety, I shall be the investigator. The one who shall observe and... eliminate." [/h1]

What is in this mysterious name: Orwell? A good plot? Realism and coherence? A branching storyline? Memorable characters? Plot twists? Perhaps, all of the mentioned and a lot more? Yes - all of the mentioned and A LOT more. This game is a very interesting game in which you'll act as an investigator working for a governmental project called "Orwell." With the help of this mass surveillance software/tool, you will be tracking and evaluating various people to identify potential "threats" to The Nation. The evaluation process includes analyzing social media accounts of the people evaluated, their chat histories, emails, phone calls, personal devices, and etc. Basically anything, which they deemed a part of their "private" life. 

What I really liked about this game is its attention to detail. On the first look, the game's storyline contains lots of unnecessary snippets of information, which might be regarded as useless by the inattentive player. However, those little details and discrepancies form a larger picture which reveals a major plot twist that takes place somewhere in the ending episodes. The plot twist itself [spoiler], which was about Juliet being the imposter instead of the suspected Harrison,[/spoiler]did make sense after some other playthroughs (accomplishing all the achievements and endings) as I've paid a lot of attention to those little details in the game. [spoiler]For me, the hint provided by Symes about Juliet's favorite book (The Mockingbird)and Harrison's lost phone seemed like the ones which can directly lead you towards the "Juliet is the true imposter" conclusion. [/spoiler]Well, the game proved to me that no story can be regarded as completely explored without the consideration of all the small details. A lesson well learnt.

As much as I liked this game, there are still things that can be improved. For instance, adding a setting for an accelerated playthrough, because DAMN, some of the calls take more than 10 minutes to finish and are unskippable. Going through the game again becomes a real pain without this feature. I understand that some events happen during phone calls (which is probably why you can't accelerate them), but as a person who finished the main plot multiple times, I don't bother to read all the stuff again. Besides, I think players decide beforehand their choices, so adding the accelerated playthrough won't hurt the experience much (it is wise to lock it until the game is completed for the first time). There were some spelling (Episode 3; objective; "motiviation") and grammar mistakes, but those are minor issues. Apart from these, there aren't much things which I'd want to be added to this game. 

I've written too much for this review already and thus will conclude my overall impression for the game. The game is truly amazing BUT is not for everyone. If you crave for action and excitement and don't like reading and analyzing, then I do not recommend this game to you. But hey! It's never a bad time to explore a new frontier and discover a little bit more about yourself. Maybe you'll love this game the same as I did and give it a thumbs up. 

[u]-QG7 Recommended[/u]

review_text_raw:
Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

review_text_raw:
Worth it? Yes. DLC? Yes. Get it on sale? Probably, but it's worth the price if you have disposable income.
I really enjoyed playing Orwell and its DLC. Here's a bullet point of stuff I think is worth knowing before you buy!

-Plot/characters are realistic in a way that would normally be mundane on their own, but this game makes it somehow feel exceptional enough to make the story worth investing in. I think this grounding to reality did a good service by this game's namesake to express the urgency and importance of privacy and compassion, IRL and online.

-Easy to navigate UI, text is usually easy to read. The news articles' text is a bit thin, but if you have a big monitory/screen it probably won't be a problem. And you typically don't need to read every word on each website and email anyway.

-Markers for unread/unused/new "datachunks" that make going back through old info much less tedious.

-Easy to immerse in because you don't have to pretend to be someone you're not to fit yourself into the world of the game. It does feel like a job, but one that has wild stuff happening and your only way to know about it is through the job. Making the player curious is really important for mystery/puzzle/investigative games, and this game did a 7/10 job with that.

-While it does take effort to make sure you're keeping up with all the info, and making sure you're not wasting resources on unimportant info; it's not overly difficult. it's not necessarily easy (the first time around), but it won't make you feel stupid if you do struggle.

-The general concept of this game is so cool to me, I wish there were a lot more games like this.

-This game is much more accessible to people who have little in-depth experience with technology. It does all the technical "hacker" type work for you, and just lets you dig through people's lives unburdened. I don't really care about all the technical stuff involved in hacking & the like, so this was a huge win for me. A game like this can flop because of poorly executed, insanely difficult to comprehend, or super unrealistic hacking mechanics; so Orwell pretty much bypassed that while still making you feel like you're putting the pieces together yourself. (As long as you don't think too hard about it, anyway.)

-It puts you in a position of being the bad guy in a situation that makes you think, "This could literally be happening IRL and I wouldn't know." This game will give you a lot to think about even after you're done playing. 

-There is an issue that happened to me twice, where I technically soft locked myself in the game, and was unable to find any answers through walkthroughs/watching others play the game. So be prepared to be very diligent when uploading info when you are not racing the clock, and don't log out for the day until you're absolutely certain you've nabbed all the important info you might need.

-This game is honestly a bit short for the sheer amount of story and world-building information available in it. I think the game should have given you more time to explore and given more options for gathering info before forcing the plot to continue, even if not all of the info is used. It holds your hand too much, but not outright.

-Overall, my biggest issues with this game have to be the fact that you can't skip or pause chats or phone calls you're observing, and it moves so fast at certain points that you don't have time to process the information you're gathering to learn about the world/characters/story. My favorite parts of this game are really just the overall experience of playing it, and the execution of concept being very clear and deliberate.

[list]
[*]A great and very frightening concept
[*]Awesome story
[*]Great replayabililty
[*]The design is just beautiful
[/list]

[*]No way to speed up dialogue you’ve already read and just need to grab info from
[/list]

[h1]Review:[/h1]
The most terrifying part of Orwell is just how easily its events could come to pass in our own world. George Orwell himself could not have predicted the level of surveillance we all voluntarily subject ourselves to by keeping always-listening, always-tracking smart devices on our persons, in our cars, and in our homes. It doesn’t take a lot of imagination to see a system such as the one portrayed in the game being used by a real nation, especially since we know the United States already conducts mass surveillance in a multitude of ways.


Orwell (the game) did an excellent job keeping me on the edge of my seat throughout its entire duration. Even though you only interact with them (or rather, their information) through a screen, it was hard not to feel connected to the characters. Whether that connection is based on sympathy or a desire to lock them up is up to you.


The game lends itself well to multiple playthroughs in order to achieve different endings, and there are tons of different ways to get to those endings. However, by the second or third time the first few chapters begin to feel very repetitive. I often found myself checking my phone while waiting for in-game conversations to finish so I could decide which chunks of data to grab. There is tons of interesting stuff to read in Orwell, but it would be nice to skip past some dialogue when I’ve already read it three times.


The length of the game really surprised me. For $11 I didn’t expect as much story and detail as I got. While it only took me about 6 hours my first time through, and I can definitely go through quicker now if I wanted, looking over all of the great little details that have been thrown in definitely takes time. That’s not a bad thing, as Orwell’s realism is only helped by how believable its characters (and their social media profiles, emails, and phone calls) are.


This is definitely a great game, and it was an awesome surprise when I discovered it while browsing the web one day. Be warned, though - after you play you’ll often find yourself thinking about your online conversations, and if something you said years ago (or even yesterday) could somehow be used to incriminate you.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

TLDR: 

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a game with a powerful concept that effectively engages with important ethical themes. Its simple mechanics can become repetitive, and minor technical issues can hinder the experience. While the narrative has strong moments, it ultimately falls short of being truly remarkable. Nevertheless, the game’s exploration of surveillance and privacy makes it a worthwhile experience for those interested in thought-provoking and socially relevant games.

Pros:

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]TL:DR: [/b] Does 1984 ring a bell? Yes? You are all good, skip this. No? Block off four hours and prepare a lighthearted movie after to flush the existential horror.

[h1]What is Orwell?[/h1]
The player takes the role of an independent third party taking the reigns of the most powerful surveillance technology ever built tasked with the investigation of a terrorist attack on a monument in the capital of a fictitious country called The Nation. Armed with a context sensitive browser the player dives head first into one medium deep rabbit hole.

[h1]Game Design | The Awesome (+2)[/h1]
I adore the brutalist functionality of the game design. It feels like a desk job. There is nothing special to it. Everything works as one would expect it to. It should feel cold. It should provide a degree of separation from the subject while not hindering gameplay. This is one of the hardest tricks any game designer can pull off. Take it from a boring person who unironically loves to create spreadsheets for any number of things. This [i]rocks[/i].

[h1]Audio design | The Terrible (-2)[/h1]
Coming in on the opposite side of the spectrum is audio design. Or lack thereof. The only notable attempt at anything are dynamic music changes when the player comes across [i]shocking[/i] new information. And yes, I am exaggerating, because the music is exaggerating. The whiplash from the norm is that great. It arrives suddenly and leaves before it had a chance to order a frickin' latte. Then there are all the missed opportunities. The player has access to various types of data from texts, to web pages, to voice calls. Instead of a transcript it would have been great to have the few calls fully voiced. It would have brought the player even closer to the characters.

[h1]Characters | The Bad (-1)[/h1]
...of which Orwell utilizes several one dimensional archetypes with a couple of exceptions that show a hint of a second dimension. Fortunately for the game, the player is not forced to linger on any of the cast. We get just as much as we need to understand from where the wind is blowing before moving on to the next person. For better or worse, commentary on surveillance killing the human experience acts as the main character of the game and is largely responsible for the ankle deep depth of the human pawns.

[h1]Closing Thoughts | The Adequate (0)[/h1]
Orwell is a tricky proposition. On one side it is concise, excellently showcases pitfalls of absolute surveillance and should be a mandatory play on any high school, on the other side it is cynical to the core and does not allow a solution of the privacy/security conundrum. I could speculate that the original intention of the authors was to show the only winning move is not to play. However, I am writing this script seven years after the release in a world that is inching closer and closer to a world of AI driven absolute surveillance. The absolute surveillance of Orwell fails even with a human at the helm of its moral compass, what chance do we have in the real world without such an agent? At the end of the day art is a reflection of our perceived reality. I understand that having no way out nets a more chilling experience. However, if the resolution does not provide a positive outlook, something to aspire to, it leaves the observer in a very dark place.

[hr][/hr]

[h4]Note[/h4]
Individual sections (and the whole game) are critiqued on a scale of [i]The Terrible (-2)[/i] from the worse to [i]The Awesome (+2)[/i].

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a detective Interactive Fiction game, where you assume a role of a goverment-employed ivestigator with an emergancy right to access citizens' devices and Internet activity.
You are tasked with finding a person responsible for a terrorist attack in a fictional city of Bonton in a fictional Nation.
The game has a really solid mechanic for gathering and sorting information, that I have personally not seen before. Your main power is collecting bits and pieces of the info in documents, on websites, in messges and voicecall transcriptions. You need to compare and analyze different sources that are often conflicting and rarely fully truthfull, keeping in mind context, biases, possible angles. The coolest parts is that instead of acting on the info, you only relay it to your supperiors who make all the calls. So in order to achieve the outcome you want, you need to basically socially ingeneer your bosses by spoon-feeding them the info that will shape their worldview. 
I feel that it's a powerful metaphor on how the perseption influences action, and how malicious forces may take advantage of the powers to shape perseption. Especially when they can control the information for the people in position of power — through media, narratives or implicit biases. 
This is the main win of the game — it explores an important concept via its engaging detective gameplay.
I do have some criticisms, or rather some notes based on my own expectations. I first came into this game expecting it to be a mostly realistic tale with a bit of the antiutopic twist. And while it certainly presents realistic aesthetic, the deeper you go into this world and plot, the more outlandish things become. This is genre fiction through and through. Observing real totalitarian regimes as they implement digital survaillance, and seeing real opposition and its struggles in such countries... Well, simplifications and assumptions Orwell makes, they just shatter believability of the whole premise. Some things just raise questions (or eybrows) even with everyday logic, such as the game's fictional geography. It somehow includes a Central-European coated country, a Slavic Eastern-European and a (sort-of) Middle-Eastern or Central-Asian (?) countiry just neighboring each others — without the cross-influence that this fact might bring. It also includes references to real states such as Germany and South Africa. A bit of a tonal clash.
But if you accept genre conventions and treat this as a pulp fiction detective story, it really opens up as a nice and fun exploration of some important topics of current society. All while being a pretty cool Interactive Fiction game.

review_text_raw:
I wrote this review on a whim after re-reading 1984, but to be sure I was assessing the game fairly I replayed the first couple of "days" (levels). I think my impressions are still accurate, and the game is still not worth playing. So on the one hand, at least the game is memorable. On the other:

In a word (one of George Orwell's own, suitably enough) the game is 'doubleplusungood'. It has very little to do with the author except for the state-surveillance meme - which was, in the first place, only "the tutorial" of 1984 - so that the game seems reluctant to explore or understand its own namesake. This is more noticeable in the sequel, which is less interested in recreating the horrifying Newspeak of 1984 ("we shall make thoughtcrime [ideological dissension] literally impossible, because there will be no words in which to express it") so much as awkwardly recreating the contemporary and vapid phenomena of 'fake news narratives'. It's cheaply political, far from the surgical satire with which George condemned his contemporary socialists, or the Isaianic fury with which he condemned the whole politically progressive enterprise. All told, the devs would have been better off writing an essay on 1984 than making two (soon to be three, I hear) shoddy video game adaptations; but should they direct their talents to original systems and concepts, I strongly believe they can make a playable game.
